title: Telling stories & real conversation
goal: Tell a simple story, link events in time, report what people said, use relative clauses with چې, and sprinkle your Pashto with natural fillers and proverbs.
intro:
Pashtuns are great storytellers. Evenings in the حجره are filled with tales of heroes and tricksters, jokes about Mullah Nasruddin, and verses of poetry — from the ancient folk couplets (لنډۍ) to Rahman Baba and Khushal Khan Khattak. A well-placed proverb (متل) can win an argument.

In this final unit you'll put everything together: the past tense, connectors that move a story along, the all-purpose word **چې**, reported speech, and the little words that make conversation sound natural.

phrases.roman: haġə́ wə́wayəl che zə stə́ṛay yəm.

Meaning what? / What do you mean?

phrases.roman: xabə́ra me pre kṛa, baṣə́na ġwā́ṛəm.

phrases.roman: obə́ che la sára xə́ṛe wi, tər pā́ya xə́ṛe wi.

grammar.title: Relative clauses with چې
grammar.body:
Pashto has no separate words for 'who', 'which', 'that' in relative clauses — it uses **چې** for all of them. The relative clause comes **after** the noun, starts with چې, and ends with its own verb:

هغه سړی **چې پرون راغی** زما تره دی
'The man **who came yesterday** is my uncle.'

The noun is often preceded by **هغه** 'that' or **دا** 'this', which signals that a relative clause is coming. When the noun is the *object* inside the relative clause, the clause follows its own rules — including ergativity in the past: هغه کتاب چې **ما** واخيست 'the book that I bought'.

چې also means 'when' (کله چې) and 'so that' (د دې لپاره چې), and after verbs of saying and thinking it means 'that'.

examples.native: هغه سړی چې پرون راغی زما تره دی.
examples.roman: haġá saṛáy che parún rā́ġay zmā trə day.
examples.en: The man who came yesterday is my uncle.

examples.native: هغه کتاب چې ما واخيست ډېر ښه دی.
examples.roman: haġá kitā́b che mā wā́xist ḍer ṣə day.
examples.en: The book I bought is very good.

examples.native: هغه نجلۍ چې سندرې وايي زما خور ده.
examples.roman: haġá njlə́y che sandə́re wā́yi zmā xor da.
examples.en: The girl who is singing is my sister.

examples.native: کله چې کور ته ورسېدم، باران شروع شو.
examples.roman: kə́la che kor ta wə́rasedəm, bārā́n shurúʿ shu.
examples.en: When I got home, it started to rain.

examples.native: ژر راغلم د دې لپاره چې تا وګورم.
examples.roman: zhər rā́ġləm də de lapā́ra che tā wə́gorəm.
examples.en: I came early so that I could see you.

grammar.title: Reported speech: keeping the original words
grammar.body:
Pashto normally reports speech **as it was said**, after **چې**, without changing pronouns or tenses the way English does:

هغه وويل چې **زه** ستړی **يم**
lit. 'He said that "I am tired"' = He said he was tired.

Only the context tells you that زه refers to 'him'. Questions are reported the same way: ما وپوښتل چې **ته** چېرته ځې؟ 'I asked where he was going' (lit. I asked: where are you going?).

Remember that **ويل** 'say' and **پوښتل** 'ask' are transitive, so in the past the speaker is oblique: **ما** وويل، **هغې** وپوښتل، **احمد** وويل. With no object, the verb takes the masculine plural form (وويل، وپوښتل).

**وايي چې** 'they say that' introduces rumours and hearsay: وايي چې سبا به باران وي.

examples.native: هغې وويل چې زه سبا نه شم راتلای.
examples.roman: haġé wə́wayəl che zə sabā́ na shəm rātlā́y.
examples.en: She said she couldn't come tomorrow.

examples.native: احمد وويل چې زه ډوډۍ نه غواړم.
examples.roman: ahmád wə́wayəl che zə ḍoḍə́y na ġwā́ṛəm.
examples.en: Ahmad said he didn't want any food.

examples.native: ما ترې وپوښتل چې ته د کوم ځای يې؟
examples.roman: mā tre wə́puṣtəl che tə də kum dzāy ye?
examples.en: I asked him where he was from.

examples.native: وايي چې دا لار خطرناکه ده.
examples.roman: wā́yi che dā lār xatarnā́ka da.
examples.en: They say this road is dangerous.

examples.native: مور مې راته وويل چې ژر کور ته راشه.
examples.roman: mor me rā́ta wə́wayəl che zhər kor ta rā́sha.
examples.en: My mother told me to come home soon.

grammar.title: Moving a story along — and sounding natural
grammar.body:
**Story connectors:**
يو وخت و … 'once upon a time …' · لومړی 'first' · بيا 'then' · وروسته له هغه 'after that' · هغه وخت 'at that time' · ناڅاپه 'suddenly' · کله چې 'when' · خو 'but' · نو 'so' · په پای کې 'in the end'.

Stories are usually told in the past, and the **imperfective past** sets the scene ('he was walking …') while the **perfective past** moves events forward ('… and suddenly he saw …').

**Fillers and reactions** that make you sound natural:
نو … 'so …' · يعنې 'I mean' · ګوره 'look' · هو کنه 'yes, exactly' · ښه؟ 'right? OK?' · واه! 'wow!' · رښتيا؟ 'really?' · څه وايې! 'you don't say!' · خير دی 'never mind' · هسې 'just, no reason'.

examples.native: يو وخت و، يو پاچا و چې درې زامن يې درلودل.
examples.roman: yaw waxt wə, yaw pāchā́ wə che dre zāmə́n ye darlodə́l.
examples.en: Once upon a time there was a king who had three sons.

examples.native: زه په لار تلم، ناڅاپه مې يو زوړ ملګری وليد.
examples.roman: zə pə lār tlə́m, nātsā́pa me yaw zoṛ malgə́ray wə́lid.
examples.en: I was walking along the road when suddenly I saw an old friend.

examples.native: لومړی موږ چای وڅښه، بيا بازار ته ووتو.
examples.roman: lumṛáy muẓ chāy wə́tsṣə, biyā́ bāzā́r ta wə́watu.
examples.en: First we drank tea, then we went out to the bazaar.
So, you mean you're not going?

dialogue.title: Grandmother's story: 'Eat, my coat!'
dialogue.setting: On a winter night, Bibi tells her grandchildren Zarlasht and Aimal a Mullah Nasruddin story.

lines.speaker: Aimal
lines.native: انا جانې، يوه کيسه راته وکړه!
lines.roman: anā́ jā́ne, yáwa kissá rā́ta wə́kṛa!
lines.en: Granny dear, tell us a story!

lines.speaker: Bibi
lines.native: ښه، واورئ. يو وخت و، ملا نصرالدين يوې مېلمستيا ته لاړ.
lines.roman: ṣə, wā́wrəy. yaw waxt wə, mullā́ nasruddín yáwe melmastyā́ ta lāṛ.
lines.en: All right, listen. Once upon a time, Mullah Nasruddin went to a feast.

lines.speaker: Bibi
lines.native: هغه زړې او چټلې جامې اغوستې وې. هېچا ورته پام ونه کړ، هېچا ورته ډوډۍ ورنه کړه.
lines.roman: haġə́ zaṛé aw chaṭə́le jā́me aġustə́le we. hechā́ wárta pām wə́na kaṛ, hechā́ wárta ḍoḍə́y wárna kṛa.
lines.en: He was wearing old, dirty clothes. Nobody paid him any attention, nobody gave him any food.

lines.speaker: Bibi
lines.native: ملا کور ته لاړ، يوه ښکلې نوې چپنه يې واغوسته او بېرته راغی.
lines.roman: mullā́ kor ta lāṛ, yáwa ṣkə́le náwe chapána ye wā́ġusta aw bérta rā́ġay.
lines.en: The Mullah went home, put on a beautiful new coat, and came back.

lines.speaker: Bibi
lines.native: اوس ټولو ورته ښه راغلاست وويل، او تر ټولو ښه ځای ته يې کېناوه.
lines.roman: os ṭolo wárta ṣə rāġlā́st wə́wayəl, aw tər ṭolo ṣə dzāy ta ye kénāwə.
lines.en: Now everyone welcomed him and seated him in the best place.

lines.speaker: Aimal
lines.en: And what did the Mullah do?

lines.speaker: Bibi
lines.native: ملا خپل لستوڼی په ښوروا کې ډوب کړ او ويې ويل: وخوره، چپنې، وخوره!
lines.roman: mullā́ xpəl lastóṇay pə ṣorwā́ ke ḍub kaṛ aw wə́ye wayəl: wə́xwra, chapáne, wə́xwra!
lines.en: The Mullah dipped his sleeve in the soup and said: 'Eat, coat, eat!'

lines.speaker: Zarlasht
lines.en: Why? As if a coat eats food?

lines.speaker: Bibi
lines.native: ملا وويل: دا مېلمستيا د چپنې لپاره ده، زما لپاره نه ده!
lines.roman: mullā́ wə́wayəl: dā melmastyā́ də chapáne lapā́ra da, zmā lapā́ra na da!
lines.en: The Mullah said: 'This feast is for the coat, not for me!'

lines.speaker: Aimal
lines.en: Ha ha! The Mullah was very clever!

lines.speaker: Bibi
lines.native: هو، متل دی چې سړی په جامو نه پېژندل کېږي. اوس ويده شئ!
lines.roman: ho, matál day che saṛáy pə jā́mo na pezhandə́l kéẓi. os widə́ shəy!
lines.en: Yes — as the saying goes, you can't judge a man by his clothes. Now off to sleep!

culture: The **landay** (لنډۍ) is the heart of Pashto folk poetry: a couplet of 9 + 13 syllables, anonymous, often sung, and traditionally composed and passed on by women. Landays speak of love, separation, war, honour and humour; one of the most famous is attributed to **Malalai of Maiwand**, the young woman who rallied Afghan fighters at the battle of Maiwand in 1880. The great poets — **Khushal Khan Khattak** (warrior-poet of honour and freedom) and **Rahman Baba** (the gentle Sufi of Peshawar, whose shrine is visited by thousands) — are quoted in everyday conversation. Learn a couple of proverbs and a landay or two, and you'll delight any Pashtun you meet. **مبارک شه** — congratulations on finishing the course!
